C0.1: Holding a note while your hands stay free is how you will tune every bass, lead and pad you build by ear.
C0.2: Knowing that an octave is a doubling lets you drop a bassline lower or lift a melody higher without guessing where it will land.
C0.3: Reading the meter keeps your bass and drums at levels you can trust, and quieter listening lets you hear the detail you are shaping.
C0.4: Spotting harmonics on the spectrum tells you why one bass sounds dull and another bright, so you can change the tone on purpose.
C1.1: Picking the right starting wave gives you a hollow lead, a buzzing bass or a pure low tone before any shaping begins.
C1.2: Tuning an oscillator by octaves, semitones and cents puts a bass in its register and stacks a musical interval above a lead.
C1.M: Copying a sound you can only hear is how you will rebuild the basses and leads you love from other tracks.
C1.3: Sweeping through a wavetable lets one held bass note change colour as it plays, the starting point for morphing, talking sounds.
C1.4: Layering a second oscillator an octave away or a few notes up makes a thin lead heavier, or turns one key into two notes.
C1.5: Slightly detuned oscillators give a held bass or pad a slow swell, and you choose how fast that swell turns.
C1.6: Stacked detuned copies turn a narrow lead into a wide, thick one, and you will know when to stop before the pitch smears.
C1.7: A quiet sub under your bass gives it steady weight, while a touch of noise adds breath and grit on top.
C1.8: Fixed phase makes each bass hit start the same way so the low end stays tight, and random phase keeps repeated notes sounding natural.
C1.9: Panning two oscillators apart spreads a lead or pad across the speakers, with a different tone on each side for extra width.
C1.C: Hearing whether a sound has a second pitch, thickness, weight or brightness lets you rebuild layered tones you come across.
